A lot of us are fed up, and that's why we're here, talking about change.

When and How are we going to start putting theory into practice?

It seems to me that for now, the best we can do is to make incremental within-system changes (e.g. start a cooperative business, engage in local political action) and sowing seeds for future large-scale changes (e.g. growing community, developing political/social theory, educating others). Part of that can be protest - it certainly seems to get people's attention, for what that's worth.

It's been important for me to get clear on what different forms of activism can reasonably be expected to achieve. A person can get burned out quickly on political protest if they're motivation stems from a belief that it will produce a positive change in the behavior of politicians or CEOs, for example. But that same person may be able to protest for years if their motivation stems from a desire to meet likeminded people and spread ideas.

Anarchism can't be implemented. If it's implemented, it's not anarchism.

Anarchism, by its very nature, has to be something to which people voluntarily come, so all any individual can do is try to live as much as possible by the ideas of anarchism and to encourage other people to do the same.

First and foremost, one should recognize and abide by the idea that all individuals are sovereign entities and should treat them as such, or more simply, one should butt the hell out of their decisions. That's really what anarchism is all about - nobody is empowered to control the lives of others, so the one thing that you can do to advance that cause is stop pretending that you should be able to control the lives of others. If everyone did that, we'd already have anarchism.

And a word of warning - if you do indeed follow that path, you'll find yourself at odds with many (I would say most) "anarchists," because their "anarchism" is really a sham, and that specifically because they never even question the presumption that other people are rightly forced to abide by their norms, and they resent having to even consider the issue. They just pretend that if the mechanism by which their preferences are imposed on other people isn't exactly identical to the current conception of a "state," that'll be sufficient.

Over time I have developed the same perspective of anarchism. Hopefully more will attain themselves to the attribute of self-sufficiency rather than dependence. I as an individual will stride myself to be dependent onto myself, though so far it has been a slow process.
